title: IF POLYGAMY IS WRONG, WHY DID GOD ALLOW ABRAHAM, JACOB, DAVID, AND SOLOMON TO HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES?
paragraphs: IF POLYGAMY IS WRONG, WHY DID GOD ALLOW ABRAHAM, JACOB, DAVID, AND SOLOMON TO HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES?

The Bible records men with many wives. Some were called righteous. Some were kings chosen by God. So was polygamy ever God's plan—or have we misunderstood the difference between what Scripture records, what God permits, and what He actually desires?
There is a question that has troubled believers, fascinated skeptics, and left more than a few Christians struggling to explain their own Bible.
And the uncomfortable part?
It's a fair question.

If marriage is supposed to be between one man and one woman, why did Abraham have Sarah and Hagar? Why did Jacob marry Leah and Rachel? Why did David have multiple wives? And why did Solomon, a king blessed with extraordinary wisdom, end up with seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines?
These weren't merely obscure men hiding in the shadows of biblical history.
Abraham was called God's friend (James 2:23).
Jacob became Israel, the father of the twelve tribes.
David was described as a man after God's own heart (Acts 13:22).
Solomon was entrusted with extraordinary wisdom.
Yet their households tell stories that would break the hearts of almost anyone who has ever loved someone, feared being replaced, experienced jealousy, or wondered whether they were enough.
So here is the question we cannot afford to avoid.
If God is holy, why does His Word contain so many stories of men practicing something Christians generally teach is contrary to His design for marriage?
Was God changing His standards?
Was He making exceptions for powerful men?

Or is there something much deeper happening in these ancient accounts—something that exposes not a contradiction in God's character, but the terrifying human tendency to confuse God's patience with God's approval?
Because once you see what is happening from Genesis to the words of Jesus Christ, you may never read these stories the same way again.
And you may discover that this question is not ultimately about how many wives a man could have.
It is about what happens when human beings take something God created to be beautiful and attempt to improve it by following their own desires.
It begins in a garden.
Not in a palace.
Not in a king's bedroom.
Not with Abraham.
Not with David.
Not with Solomon.

In a garden, before sin entered the world, before jealousy poisoned relationships, before women competed for affection, and before powerful men began treating marriage as an instrument of wealth, political influence, or personal gratification.
Genesis 2:24 declares:
"Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh." (KJV)
The Hebrew reads:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Al-ken ya'azov ish et-aviv ve'et-immo, vedavaq be'ishto, vehayu levasar echad.
The final words matter enormously.
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד — vehayu levasar echad.
"And they shall become one flesh."
The Hebrew word echad means "one." In this passage, the expression describes the profound union formed through marriage.
But we must be careful here.

The Hebrew word echad by itself does not prove monogamy. Scripture uses the word "one" in different contexts, and forcing it to carry an argument it was never intended to carry would weaken rather than strengthen biblical interpretation.
The force of Genesis 2:24 comes from the entire creation narrative.
God creates the man.
God creates the woman.
God brings them together.
And Scripture presents their union as the foundational pattern of marriage.
One man.
One woman.
A covenantal union described as becoming one flesh.
There is no rivalry for Adam's affection.
No second wife standing outside the garden.
No woman wondering whether she will be loved tomorrow.
No household divided into competing mothers and children.
The picture is not of a man collecting wives.
It is of two people joined together.
And centuries later, when religious leaders questioned Jesus about marriage and divorce, He did something extraordinary.
He did not begin with the customs of Abraham.
He did not appeal to the royal household of David.
He did not point to Solomon's wealth or wisdom.
He went back to creation.
Jesus said:
"Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female,
And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." (Matthew 19:4–6, KJV)
Notice what Jesus did.
He interpreted marriage by returning to what God established "at the beginning."
The Greek of Matthew 19:5 includes the words:
καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
Kai esontai hoi dyo eis sarka mian.
"And the two shall become one flesh."
There is a word in Jesus' quotation that deserves our attention.
δύο — dyo.
"Two."
Jesus explicitly speaks of the two becoming one flesh.
His immediate subject is divorce, not a direct debate over polygamy. We should not pretend otherwise.
But His appeal to the original creation pattern is foundational to the Christian understanding of marriage as an exclusive union between one man and one woman.
When Jesus was asked to explain what marriage should be, He pointed beyond the complicated arrangements tolerated throughout Israel's history.
He pointed back to God's beginning.
And that distinction changes everything.
The Bible can truthfully describe what people did without declaring that everything they did was righteous.
Read that again.
Because much of the confusion disappears when we learn to distinguish between biblical description and biblical prescription.
Description tells us what happened.
Prescription tells us what ought to happen.
Scripture records murder.
That does not make murder holy.
It records adultery.
That does not make adultery acceptable.
It records deception, slavery, idolatry, betrayal, drunkenness, violence, and the exploitation of vulnerable people.
But recording these things is not the same as commanding or celebrating them.
The Bible is remarkably honest about the people God worked through.
And that honesty is one reason its stories can be so unsettling.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It does not conceal their moral failures to protect their reputations.
It tells us that Abraham believed God—and also acted out of fear.
It tells us that David worshiped God—and also committed terrible sins.
It tells us that Solomon received wisdom—and later allowed his heart to turn away.
The Bible is not a collection of perfect people demonstrating their perfection.
It is the unfolding revelation of a holy God working in a world profoundly damaged by sin.
And when we examine the earliest biblical account of polygamy, the setting should make us uncomfortable.
The first man explicitly described as taking two wives is not Abraham.
It is Lamech.
Genesis 4:19 says:
"And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah." (KJV)
Lamech appears in the line of Cain, in a narrative that also records his boast about killing a man and his escalating language of vengeance (Genesis 4:23–24).
This does not mean the text explicitly says his two marriages caused his violence.
It does not.
But it is significant that the Bible first introduces plural marriage in a morally troubled context rather than in the original creation account.
And as the biblical story unfolds, the repeated household conflicts become difficult to ignore.
Consider Abraham.
God promised him descendants.
God promised that his offspring would become a great nation.
But years passed.
Sarah remained unable to conceive.
And waiting became painful.
Genesis 16 tells us that Sarah gave her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abraham as a wife so that they might obtain a child through her.
This arrangement reflected a recognizable ancient social practice.
But the fact that something was culturally practiced did not make its consequences harmless.
Hagar conceived.
And almost immediately, the household began to fracture.
Genesis 16:4 records that after Hagar conceived, Sarah was despised in her eyes, as the KJV renders it.
Sarah responded with anger.
Abraham failed to resolve the conflict justly.
Hagar was treated harshly.
And she fled.
Imagine the scene.
One woman desperate for a child.
Another woman placed into a situation shaped by her mistress's expectations and her master's authority.
A husband caught in a conflict that should never be reduced to a simple love triangle.
And an unborn child whose future was entangled in adult decisions he did not make.
This is not a romantic celebration of plural marriage.
It is a deeply painful account of impatience, power, vulnerability, and broken relationships.
Yet something beautiful happens in the middle of that tragedy.
God sees Hagar.
Not merely Sarah.
Not merely Abraham.
Hagar.
A foreign woman.
A servant.
A person whose suffering could easily have been overlooked.
Genesis 16:13 records her response to the Lord who spoke to her.
She identifies Him as the God who sees her.
The Hebrew expression associated with this passage is:
אֵל רֳאִי — El Ro'i.
Commonly understood as "God who sees me," although the precise nuance of the Hebrew phrase has been discussed by interpreters.
Do not miss the beauty of this.
God's care for Hagar does not mean He approved every decision that placed her in that situation.
It means human failure did not place her beyond His compassion.
The God of Scripture was not blind to the woman suffering inside the household of a man of faith.
And perhaps someone reading this knows what that feels like.
To be caught in somebody else's decisions.
To suffer because someone with greater power chose what benefited them.
To feel like the overlooked person in a story where everyone else seems more important.
Hagar's account reminds us that God sees people whom society may ignore.
But the consequences within Abraham's household did not simply disappear.
Years later, the tensions surrounding Isaac and Ishmael resulted in another heartbreaking separation (Genesis 21:8–21).
God continued to care for Hagar and Ishmael.
But the family still experienced pain.
That is an important biblical distinction.
God's faithfulness to people living with the consequences of human decisions is not the same as God's approval of those decisions.
Now consider Jacob.
If Abraham's household makes you uncomfortable, Jacob's household may leave you heartbroken.
Jacob loved Rachel.
He worked seven years to marry her.
Genesis 29:20 says those years seemed like only a few days because of his love for her.
There is something deeply moving about that description.
Seven years of labor.
Seven years of anticipation.
Seven years of looking forward to building a life with the woman he loved.
Then came the wedding.
And the deception.
Laban gave Leah to Jacob instead.
Jacob later married Rachel as well.
And what followed was not the beautiful family arrangement that romanticized portrayals of polygamy might lead us to expect.
It was a household filled with painful comparison.
Genesis 29:30 says Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
Imagine being Leah.
Married.
Present.
Giving your life to a family.
Yet knowing your husband loved another woman more.
Imagine waking up beside a man whose heart was elsewhere.
Imagine bearing children while hoping that each birth might finally make him love you.
Genesis 29:32 records Leah saying:
"Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me." (KJV)
There is an entire lifetime of emotional longing inside that sentence.
"Now therefore my husband will love me."
Not simply, "I have a son."
Not simply, "God has blessed me."
But perhaps now...
Perhaps after this child...
Perhaps after I give him something valuable...
He will love me.
How many people today are still living with that same aching question?
What more must I do to be chosen?
What more must I give to be enough?
How much of myself must I surrender before someone finally loves me without comparison?
Leah's pain was real.
Rachel's pain was real too.
Rachel struggled with infertility while watching her sister bear children.
Genesis 30:1 records Rachel saying to Jacob:
"Give me children, or else I die." (KJV)
That is not the language of a peaceful household.
It is the cry of a woman overwhelmed by grief and desperation.
Eventually, the family arrangement expanded through Bilhah and Zilpah, the servants of Rachel and Leah.
The women and children became caught in a complicated struggle over fertility, status, and affection.
The text does not invite us to celebrate this rivalry.
It invites us to see the suffering.
And yet God continued working through that deeply imperfect family.
The sons born within it became the ancestors of Israel's tribes.
Does that mean God endorsed every part of the arrangement?
No.
It means God's redemptive purposes were not defeated by the failures of the people through whom He worked.
That distinction is essential.
God can bring redemption out of a broken situation without calling the brokenness good.
Then we come to David.
A man who loved God.
A musician.
A shepherd.
A warrior.
A king.
A man who wrote psalms that still comfort suffering believers thousands of years later.
And a man whose personal failures caused extraordinary devastation.
David had multiple wives, as passages such as 2 Samuel 3:2–5 and 5:13 make clear.
But Scripture never tells us that his accumulation of wives was the reason God loved him.
In fact, Deuteronomy 17:17 had already warned Israel's future kings:
"Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away." (KJV)
This matters because some people argue that the Old Testament simply treated unlimited polygamy as a divine ideal.
It did not.
The law contained restrictions that acknowledged plural marriages within Israelite society.
Exodus 21:10, for example, protected a wife's rights to food, clothing, and marital obligations if another wife was taken.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17 regulated inheritance in a household with two wives, preventing a father from unjustly depriving his firstborn son because he preferred another wife.
These laws are important because they show that the issue is more complicated than saying the Old Testament explicitly prohibited every instance of polygamy.
It did not.
Plural marriage was tolerated and regulated in ancient Israel.
But regulation is not necessarily endorsement as an ideal.
Laws addressing difficult social realities can restrain injustice without presenting those realities as the fullest expression of God's intention.
Jesus Himself gives us a vital interpretive principle in Matthew 19:8.
When discussing Moses' permission concerning divorce, He explains that this concession was related to hardness of heart.
Then He says:
"But from the beginning it was not so." (KJV)
Jesus is speaking specifically about divorce.
We should not claim that He explicitly applied that statement to every Old Testament plural marriage.

Nevertheless, His distinction between an accommodated practice and God's original intention helps us understand why Christians look to creation and Christ's teaching when discerning the design of marriage.
Now return to David.
His story contains an especially devastating example of what happens when power is used to take what belongs to another.
In 2 Samuel 11, David saw Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah.
He sent for her.
He slept with her.
She became pregnant.
And David eventually arranged circumstances that led to Uriah's death.
This was not simply another episode of polygamy.
It was an abuse of royal power, adultery, and a grave act of injustice.
The prophet Nathan confronted David.
And the consequences were severe.
The biblical narrative does not treat David's status as king as permission to escape moral accountability.
He was chosen.
He was gifted.
He was powerful.
And he was still answerable to God.
The lesson is uncomfortable because it exposes something that religious people sometimes forget.
Being used by God does not mean every choice you make is approved by God.
Spiritual gifts are not proof of moral perfection.
Public ministry is not a substitute for private obedience.
A beautiful worship song does not erase an act of injustice.
And a title, a platform, or a reputation for faith cannot make sin righteous.
David's life teaches us that a person can genuinely love God and still commit grievous evil.
That does not excuse the evil.
It makes repentance necessary.
Psalm 51, traditionally associated with David's repentance after Nathan confronted him, gives us words that reveal the proper response to sin.
"Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." (Psalm 51:10, KJV)
Not, "God, explain why my position makes this acceptable."
Not, "Everyone else was doing it."
Not, "I have done too much for You to be judged."
But:
"Create in me a clean heart."
And this brings us to Solomon.
Perhaps no biblical figure illustrates the danger of multiplied wives more explicitly.
Solomon began with extraordinary privileges.
God gave him wisdom.
He built the temple.
He possessed wealth and influence.
Yet 1 Kings 11:3 records:
"And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart." (KJV)
The passage is painfully direct.
His wives turned away his heart.
The surrounding verses explain that his marriages to foreign women were connected with his participation in the worship of other gods, contrary to God's commands.
The point is not that foreign women as an ethnic group were inherently corrupt.
The text's concern is covenant unfaithfulness and idolatry.
Nor does the passage teach that every woman Solomon married was personally responsible for his sin.
Solomon himself was accountable for his decisions.
He multiplied wives despite the warning given to Israel's kings.
He allowed competing loyalties to draw his heart away from the Lord.
The man who possessed extraordinary wisdom still needed obedience.
The man who built the temple still needed faithfulness.
The man who understood so much still failed to guard his own heart.
And there is something deeply sobering about that.
You can know Scripture and still disobey it.
You can understand theology and still justify your desires.
You can speak beautifully about God while quietly making compromises that are destroying your spiritual life.
Solomon's tragedy was not a lack of information.
It was a failure of faithfulness.
And perhaps this is where the question about polygamy begins to reach beyond ancient marriage customs.
Because human beings still do this.
We search Scripture for permission to keep what we do not want to surrender.
We find a flawed biblical character and say, "But he did it."
We point to someone's blessing and assume everything in that person's life must have God's approval.
We confuse God's mercy with His endorsement.
And sometimes we are less interested in what God actually desires than in how much of our own desire we can keep while still calling ourselves obedient.
That is not merely an ancient problem.
It is a human problem.
But someone may still raise a difficult objection.
"What about 2 Samuel 12:8? Doesn't God say He gave David his master's wives?"
That question deserves a serious answer.
In Nathan's confrontation with David, God speaks of giving him his master's house and his master's wives into his bosom, as the KJV renders the passage.
This language cannot simply be ignored.
It is part of Scripture.
The verse occurs in a royal context, where the transfer of a predecessor's household could symbolize the transfer of royal status and authority.

Interpreters differ over whether the statement should be understood as a literal transfer of Saul's wives to David or as language representing the royal household and privileges associated with kingship.
The passage does not independently establish that every royal marriage was God's original ideal.
But neither should we pretend the verse is absent or easy.
A faithful interpretation must hold it alongside Genesis 2:24, Deuteronomy 17:17, the regulations of Mosaic law, the prophetic warnings, and Jesus' teaching about marriage.
And we should acknowledge another important distinction.
The Old Testament does not consistently describe every plural marriage as a personal sin in the same way it explicitly condemns adultery.
Its legal treatment of polygamy is more nuanced than that.

The Christian conclusion that monogamy expresses God's design for marriage is drawn from the broader canonical witness, especially creation and the teaching of Christ, rather than from pretending there is a single Old Testament verse that simply says, "Every man with more than one wife is guilty of adultery."
Biblical faithfulness requires honesty about what the text says—and what it does not say.
We do not honor God by making Scripture appear simpler than it is.
We honor Him by handling it truthfully.
And that includes another challenging observation.
God did not abandon Abraham.
He did not erase Jacob.
He did not remove David's psalms from Scripture.
He did not pretend Solomon never existed.
But neither did He conceal their failures.
Why?
Because God's redemptive story is not built on the moral perfection of Abraham, Jacob, David, or Solomon.
It is ultimately fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
And this is where everything changes.
Jesus did not come merely to settle an ancient argument about marriage arrangements.
He came to redeem sinners and restore people to God.
The apostle Paul describes marriage in Ephesians 5:31–32 by quoting the one-flesh language of Genesis and then connecting it to Christ and the church.
He writes:
This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church." (KJV)
Notice the pattern.
The two become one flesh.
And Paul sees in marriage a profound relationship to the covenantal union between Christ and His people.
Christian marriage is therefore not merely a private arrangement for fulfilling personal desires.
It is called to reflect faithful, sacrificial, covenantal love.
That is why the New Testament repeatedly places such emphasis on marital faithfulness.
In 1 Corinthians 7:2, Paul speaks of each man having his own wife and each woman her own husband.

In 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6, church overseers are described using the expression commonly translated "the husband of one wife," with interpretive discussion about the full implications of that qualification.
These passages belong to the wider New Testament picture of marital fidelity, self-control, and covenant responsibility.
And when we look at Jesus Himself, we encounter something more beautiful than the accumulation of relationships for personal advantage.
We encounter the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His bride.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
That is the opposite of using another person merely to satisfy one's own desires.
Christ does not exploit His bride.
He sacrifices Himself for her.
He does not treat her as disposable.
He loves her with covenantal faithfulness.
He does not seek power over her for selfish gain.
He gives Himself for her good.
And that changes the question.
Instead of asking, "How many wives did ancient men manage to have?"
We should be asking, "What kind of love does God call us to practice?"
Instead of searching for loopholes in the stories of flawed men, we should be looking to the character of the sinless Savior.
Because Abraham was not our perfect example.
Jacob was not our perfect example.
David was not our perfect example.
Solomon was not our perfect example.
Jesus is.
And Jesus did not come to teach us how to justify our selfishness.
He came to save us from sin and transform the way we live.
Perhaps you are reading this because someone challenged your faith with this very question.
Perhaps a skeptic asked you why the Bible seems to tolerate something Christians now reject, and you did not know how to answer.
You do not have to be ashamed of asking difficult questions.
Christian faith does not require pretending the hard passages are not there.
It requires approaching them with honesty, humility, and a willingness to let Scripture speak in its full context.
Perhaps you are not struggling with a theological question at all.
Perhaps you know what it means to be Leah.
To love someone who keeps comparing you to somebody else.
To feel invisible inside a relationship.
To give and give while wondering whether you will ever be enough.
Perhaps you know what it means to be Hagar.
To live with the consequences of decisions you did not control.
To feel pushed aside when your presence becomes inconvenient.
Perhaps you know what it means to be Rachel.
To carry an ache that others do not understand.
To watch someone else receive what you have desperately prayed for.
Or perhaps, if you are willing to be painfully honest, you recognize something of David or Solomon in yourself.
Not necessarily their particular sins.
But their capacity to know what is right while choosing what is wrong.
Their temptation to mistake privilege for permission.
Their ability to justify what they should have surrendered.
And maybe the most important question today is not whether Abraham had more than one wife.
Maybe it is whether you have been using somebody else's broken story to excuse what God is asking you to confront in your own.
That question reaches all of us.
Because none of us comes to Christ with a flawless record.
We come carrying pride.
Fear.
Regret.
Compromise.
Wounds.
Secret failures.
Sometimes the consequences of our own choices.
Sometimes the consequences of someone else's.
But the Gospel tells us that sin does not have to be the final word over a repentant sinner's life.
Jesus Christ died for our sins and rose again.
His grace is not permission to continue in rebellion.
It is the mercy that calls us out of rebellion and into new life.
And forgiveness does not mean that every earthly consequence disappears.
Abraham's family still experienced division.
Jacob's household still experienced rivalry.
David's sins still brought suffering.
Solomon's choices still had consequences.
But the Bible's message does not end with the failures of these men.
It moves toward the faithfulness of Christ.
The One who never sinned.
The One who never exploited another person.
The One who never betrayed His Father's will.
The One who offered Himself to redeem those who could never redeem themselves.
That is why the theme of Scripture is not simply the scandal of human failure.
It is the grace of God revealed most fully in Jesus Christ.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by rewriting history to protect the reputations of biblical heroes.
But by entering a world filled with sin and offering redemption through His own death and resurrection.
And here is something I hope you never forget.
The Bible's honesty about the failures of its most celebrated figures is not a weakness that needs to be hidden.
It is part of the testimony that no human hero can take the place of Jesus.
If the Bible were simply trying to manufacture flawless legends, its portraits of the patriarchs and kings would be very different.
Instead, it shows us their failures with startling candor.
And it keeps directing our attention beyond them.
To the God who remains faithful.
To the Savior who is without sin.
To the grace that calls sinners to repentance.
To the transformation that begins when we stop defending our darkness and bring it into His light.
So if someone asks you again, "If polygamy is wrong, why did so many men in the Bible have multiple wives?" you can answer without evasion.
The Old Testament records plural marriages because they were part of the real social and historical world in which God's redemptive purposes unfolded.
The Mosaic law regulated such marriages and sought to restrain certain injustices within them.
Scripture also repeatedly portrays painful rivalry, family division, and spiritual danger within these households.
God's original creation account presents the union of man and woman as one flesh, and Jesus explicitly returns to that beginning as the foundation of His teaching on marriage.
The Bible does not demand that we imitate every action of every person God used.
It calls us to understand those people in light of God's revealed purposes—and ultimately in light of Jesus Christ.
And if you are married, let this truth challenge you beyond the argument.
Do not use another person's failure as permission to become unfaithful.
Do not make your spouse compete for the love and loyalty that your covenant requires.
Do not confuse being desired with being loved.
Do not treat another human being as a possession.
Love with integrity.
Practice faithfulness.
Repent when you have done wrong.
Seek help when a relationship is being damaged.
And remember that forgiveness never requires someone to remain in abuse or danger.
If you are single, your worth is not measured by whether someone has chosen you.
If you are divorced, widowed, abandoned, or carrying the grief of a broken relationship, your life is not beyond God's compassion or His redemptive work.
If you have failed sexually or relationally, do not turn God's mercy into an excuse.
Bring your sin to Christ.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Receive the forgiveness He offers.
And begin walking in obedience, one faithful step at a time.
Because the deepest miracle of the Gospel is not that God found a world filled with perfect people.
It is that Christ came to save sinners.
And that includes people whose stories are complicated.
People whose families are fractured.
People whose past is embarrassing.
People whose questions are difficult.
People who have been wounded by others.
And people who must finally admit that they have wounded others too.
There is room at the foot of the cross for honest repentance.
There is grace for the sinner who turns to Christ.
There is hope for the person who has spent years believing that the worst chapter of their life must be the final chapter.
But do not confuse grace with a license to remain unchanged.
The same Jesus who receives repentant sinners calls them to follow Him.
And following Him means allowing His truth to challenge even the things we have spent years defending.
So let me ask you something personal.
When you read the stories of Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon, what speaks most deeply to you?
Is it the courage to ask difficult questions about Scripture?
The pain of the women whose stories are often overlooked?
The warning that spiritual privilege does not excuse disobedience?
Or the hope that God can still work redemptively through a life marked by failure?
Not simply to win an argument.
Not to shame someone who sees the passage differently.
But because thoughtful, honest conversations about Scripture can help people grow in their understanding of Christ.
And if you are wrestling with a painful question about the Bible, write that question. You do not have to pretend that faith means never struggling to understand.
Someone else may be carrying the same question in silence.
And perhaps your willingness to ask it will help them seek the truth too.
You may need to return to these passages when the question comes up again.
Our desire is not to produce content that merely wins attention.
It is to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, grow in discernment, repent where necessary, and walk more faithfully with Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond occasional inspiration into deeper biblical understanding, prayer, spiritual growth, and daily discipleship.
It is one practical way to partner with the work.
Scripture teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
That is the spirit in which we invite support.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
But the deepest value of supporting Gospel ministry is not a discount or a product.
It is the opportunity to participate in helping biblical truth reach people who are hungry for it.
Some are believers seeking maturity.
Some are exhausted Christians trying to find their way back to prayer.
Some are skeptics who have never heard a careful answer to their questions.
Some are carrying shame and need to understand what repentance and forgiveness really mean.
And some may be one honest conversation away from opening the Scriptures for themselves.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep asking questions.
Keep growing in Christ.
No one has to pay to be worthy of God's love.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And the reason we labor to share that message is precisely because no human being can purchase what Christ accomplished through His sacrifice.
So come back to the question that started this entire conversation.
Why did so many men in the Bible have multiple wives?
Because Scripture tells the truth about a fallen world, including the complicated practices of the people through whom God's redemptive history unfolded.
Why does Jesus return to the beginning?
Because God's design is not finally determined by the compromises people make along the way.
And why does any of this matter to you and me?
Because every generation faces the same temptation.
To look at what God has tolerated and call it what God desires.
To look at what someone else got away with and call it permission.
To look at a blessed person's life and assume every choice they made was holy.
But the cross confronts our excuses.
The resurrection announces our hope.
And the words of Jesus call us back to truth.
You do not have to defend Abraham's every decision to believe in Abraham's God.
You do not have to justify David's every action to treasure David's psalms.
You do not have to excuse Solomon's failures to learn from his wisdom.
And you do not have to pretend your own past was righteous in order to receive the mercy of Jesus Christ.
The Bible does not hide the scandals of its heroes.
It reveals the Savior who is greater than every one of them.
And perhaps that is the truth someone needs to hear tonight.
God did not preserve their broken stories so we would have permission to repeat their sins, but so we would learn to place our hope in the Savior who never sinned.
